Faulkner County housing and towns

Central Arkansas is home to Faulkner County, where Conway serves as both seat and biggest city. The 2020 population was 123,498, fifth highest among Arkansas counties. Interstate 40 made Conway and the towns around it commuter communities for Little Rock, and that steady demand is part of what shapes house prices here.

Mayflower, Vilonia, Greenbrier, Guy, Holland, Enola, Mount Vernon, Quitman, Wooster and Damascus are separate towns. Greenbrier and Vilonia have their own schools and city rules. Before you compare bills with a neighbor, check which school district and city appear on yours.

Assessor and Collector offices

Two county offices shape your bill. One sets the value and the other sends the statement and takes the money. The Assessor is at 806 Faulkner Street in Conway, phone 501-450-4905, with a second location at 89 N Broadview Street in Greenbrier. The office is open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. until 4:30 p.m.

The Collector's phone is 501-450-4921. Conway keeps the same weekday schedule. The Greenbrier office at 89 N Broadview Street opens earlier on Monday through Thursday, 7:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and closes at noon on Friday after opening at 8:00 a.m.

  • Mail, in-person and online payments are all taken.
  • Online payments go through actdatascout.com/faulknerar, and a card fee applies.
  • Pay personal property tax first or together with real estate tax. An electronic real estate payment is refused until the personal property bill is cleared.
  • Statements are mailed in spring. If nothing has arrived by July 1, phone the Collector.

Due dates and penalties

Taxes here run one year behind, so what you pay now covers the prior year's assessment. The collection season starts March 1 and closes October 15, and a weekend or holiday on the last day pushes it to the next business day.

Anything paid after October 15 draws a 10 percent penalty on both real estate and personal property. Late real estate tax carries 10 percent annual interest on top.

Reappraisal and how to appeal

The Assessor expects the current reappraisal cycle to wrap up in 2028. Arkansas counties reappraise every 3, 4 or 5 years. Asking which year crews last covered your neighborhood tells you when your value is likely to move.

Appraisers generally stay outside. Interior rooms are not inspected and measurements are approximate, so read your property record for wrong square footage or missing features.

Call the Assessor first, since a plain data mistake may be corrected with no hearing at all. Still unhappy? Request a hearing before the County Board of Equalization. Its five members equalize assessed values under Arkansas Code 26-27-301 through 26-27-325, and the third Monday in August is the last day to get on the schedule. Take photos of defects, repair estimates and recent sales of comparable houses nearby.

Homestead credit

If you live in the house, you can claim a homestead credit worth up to $600 a year. The application for the current tax bill is due October 15. Check your bill, or call the Collector, for the exact amount.

Owners 65 or older, or totally disabled, may qualify for a freeze on the taxable value of a principal residence. Both benefits follow the person living there. A buyer has to reapply after moving in, so neither transfers with the deed, and the first bill the buyer sees can run higher than yours.

Storm damage and repair records

The April 27, 2014 tornado, rated EF4, destroyed or heavily damaged homes in Mayflower and Vilonia, including the Parkwood Meadows subdivision in Vilonia and the River Plantation subdivision in Mayflower. Twelve of its 16 deaths were in Faulkner County. Homes along Lake Conway were also damaged.

Buyers in these areas ask about past storms, and a clear answer helps a sale move along.

  • Say whether the roof, slab or storm shelter was rebuilt after a past storm.
  • Keep permit records for repairs.
  • Photograph damage you did not repair, since buyers will ask.

If your house has storm repairs or unpermitted work

Open-ended questions slow a sale more than the repairs themselves. If a contractor fixed the roof after hail or wind, find the invoice. If you added a deck, carport or storage building, look for the permit. A missing permit does not end a sale, but telling a buyer early lets them price it in rather than discover it during an inspection.

A buyer paying cash can take the house as it stands and adjust the price for what needs work. A buyer with a lender usually cannot, because an appraisal and inspection feed the loan decision. That difference is the main reason owners of storm-worn or heavily used houses look at direct sales.

Recording a sale

Deeds are recorded by the Circuit Clerk, who acts as ex-officio recorder, at 724 Locust Avenue in Conway, phone 501-450-4911. Budget $15 for page one of a deed and $5 for each page after that, while a plat or survey runs $15.

Land records are online, and the clerk lists e-recording vendors that title companies use to file without a trip to the courthouse. You can also sign up for a free email alert that fires when a document is indexed under your name. Arkansas also taxes the transfer at $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration. Records can be searched at ARCountyData.com and ActDataScout.com, which the Assessor says update monthly.

What to gather before you list

A few documents save time once an offer arrives. Pull your last tax statement and the receipt showing it was paid. Find the deed, any survey or plat, and permit paperwork for roof, slab or storm shelter work. If you claimed the homestead credit or the senior freeze, note that the new owner starts fresh.

Call the Assessor to confirm the parcel number and acreage on file, and ask the clerk whether any older instruments are indexed against the property. Cleaning up a mismatch before a buyer finds it keeps the timeline short and avoids a last-minute delay at the title company.

Sellers who live outside the county, such as heirs, can handle most of this by phone and email. Because records are searchable from home, an heir in another state seldom needs to visit Conway in person.

How a closing usually moves

After you accept an offer, the title company opens an order and runs a search on the property. The search turns up unpaid taxes, liens and any recorded problems. You then receive a settlement statement listing the tax payoff, recording fees and the transfer tax.

On closing day you sign the deed. The title company records it with the Circuit Clerk and pays off the tax balance from proceeds. With a cash buyer and a clean title search, this can finish on a date you choose rather than on a lender's schedule.

Selling with taxes owed

Because the county bills a year behind, a closing often lands while some tax is still owed. Get the parcel's balance from the Collector, with any penalty and interest included, and hand it to the title company. The balance comes out of your sale proceeds, and the settlement statement shows how the year's bill is split with the buyer.

If you owe personal property tax, settle it first. An unpaid personal property balance blocks the electronic real estate payment, and that can slow the payoff.

A cash sale skips showings, appraisals and repair requests. The tax payoff and the recording steps do not change. Set any written offer next to your payoff figure to see what you would walk away with.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I pay my Faulkner County tax bill?

The Collector takes payment at the Conway courthouse office, at the Greenbrier branch, through the mail and online. Call 501-450-4921 with questions.

How much is the late charge in Faulkner County?

Ten percent, applied after October 15. Real estate tax also accrues 10 percent annual interest.

Can I pay Faulkner County real estate tax online?

Yes, through actdatascout.com/faulknerar with a card fee. Personal property tax has to be paid first, because real estate cannot be paid electronically until it is.

When will Faulkner County finish its current reappraisal?

The Assessor says 2028. Ask which year your neighborhood was last visited.

Will the buyer inherit my homestead credit?

No. The new owner files a fresh application after moving in.

Garland County and its school districts

Thermal springs, lakes and the Ouachita Mountains define Garland County, and Hot Springs serves as seat and biggest city. About 100,180 people lived here in 2020, spread over 735 square miles that include 57 of water. Lake Hamilton, Hot Springs Village, Rockwell, Piney, Mountain Pine, Fountain Lake and Lonsdale show up on the county map.

Five public school districts serve the city: Hot Springs, Lakeside, Cutter-Morning Star, Fountain Lake and Lake Hamilton. The district your house sits in sets part of the millage, so a house a few streets over can carry a different bill.

Property near the national park and lakes

Hot Springs National Park is the only national park in Arkansas, and the National Park Service manages it. Congress set aside the Hot Springs Reservation in 1832, the park was established in 1921, and a property dispute was settled in the federal government's favor by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1877. That history puts a federal boundary in the middle of the county seat.

If your house sits close to the park line or a lake shore, order a survey and ask the title company to look for easements or federal interests. A neighbor's description of the boundary is not a substitute for the recorded record.

Eight bathhouses stand along Central Avenue on Bathhouse Row, and that downtown stretch carries its own constraints. If your house is in an older part of town, ask the title company whether any recorded restriction or easement runs with the lot. Buyers' lenders tend to ask, and an answer ready in advance saves days.

Assessor and Tax Collector

The Assessor values property and the Tax Collector bills it. You will find both in the Government Office Building at 200 Woodbine Street, Hot Springs. The Assessor is at Suite 123, phone 501-622-3730.

The Tax Collector has been reported at Suite 108 with a 24-hour drop box behind the building, and the county's online payment page lists 501-622-3710. Call before you make a trip to confirm the office and its hours. The courthouse is at 501 Ouachita Avenue, phone 501-622-3600, and the county homepage has a tax and payment lookup on its quick links.

Due dates and penalties

The real estate deadline is October 15, moving to the next business day when it lands on a weekend or holiday. Partial payments are generally accepted along the way. The county has charged a 3.8 percent card convenience fee that it does not keep, so ask what the current fee is before paying by card.

The owner of record on January 1 is the person assessed. After a sale, the recorded deed is what puts the buyer's name on the roll, which is why timely recording matters.

Deadline or stepDateWhat it means

Penalty and fee amounts can change, so confirm them with the collector.

Reappraisal, caps and appeals

The state requires reappraisal on a 3, 4 or 5 year schedule. Garland County reported a five-year cycle in 2019 and hired an outside appraisal firm. Assessed value runs at 20 percent of market value.

Under Amendment 79, assessed value is frozen for owner-occupied homes of seniors and disabled owners, and yearly increases on owner-occupied homes cannot exceed 5 percent. So a house that gained more than 25 percent over a five-year cycle is not taxed at its full new value the moment the next cycle ends.

Think the value is off? Phone the Assessor, because wrong square footage or room counts can be fixed informally. A real disagreement over value goes to the County Board of Equalization, and you must schedule by the third Monday in August.

Millage can differ by town

Millage varies from one town to the next. In late 2019 the Quorum Court ratified rates that included a rollback for Mountain Pine's general fund, from 5 mills to 4.9 mills. State law requires a rollback when a tax base grows by more than 10 percent, and Mountain Pine's taxable assessed value had risen 11.51 percent, helped by close to $1 million in new construction, mostly a plant finished in 2018 and assessed in 2019.

A new plant, subdivision or lake development can move a bill. If you are comparing parcels, ask for the current millage for the specific school district and city.

Selling with taxes owed

Request a statement for the parcel from the Collector and let the title company settle the balance out of proceeds. The Garland County Circuit Clerk records the deed. A state transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration applies to deals above $100.

Taxes left unpaid can lead to an auction of delinquent land by the Commissioner of State Lands. Act 241, effective July 1, 2023, made auction sales final. The redemption right ends at 4 p.m. on the last business day before the sale, so clear any delinquency well ahead of that.

  • Order a survey when the lot is near a lake or the park boundary.
  • Check the school district and any improvement district on the bill.
  • Collect permits for lakefront or older downtown work.
  • Ask the Tax Collector whether a prior-year balance or penalty is attached to the parcel.
  • Photograph any repairs you finished so a buyer can see the condition.

From offer to closing

After you shake hands on a price, a title company opens a file and searches the parcel record. It turns up the tax balance, liens and recorded easements. Expect a few questions about who holds title, whether a lake or park boundary touches the lot and whether an improvement district charge sits on the bill.

Closing day is mostly signing. The deed goes to the Circuit Clerk, the Collector gets paid from proceeds, and the next bill belongs to the buyer once the deed is on record.

An heir selling from another state can do nearly all of this by phone and mail. Request the balance in writing and keep the receipt.

What a cash sale skips

A regular listing in Hot Springs brings repairs, showings, an inspection and a lender's appraisal. Rain adds to it: the area gets about 58 inches a year and May is the wettest month, so roofs, crawl spaces and grading on older downtown and lakefront houses draw a close look.

A cash buyer who takes the house as is drops the repair list. Tax payoff, recording and disclosure still happen. What changes is the calendar: closing follows your date, which suits heirs, relocating owners and anyone carrying two houses.

Have your last tax statement, deed, any survey and permit records ready. Lay the written offer beside the tax payoff to see your net.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Garland County Assessor?

Go to 200 Woodbine, Suite 123, Hot Springs, AR 71901, or call 501-622-3730.

When is the Garland County property tax deadline?

October 15. A weekend or holiday moves it to the next business day, and partial payments are generally accepted.

How do I appeal a Garland County assessment?

Talk to the Assessor, then ask for a Board of Equalization hearing before the third Monday in August.

Is land inside Hot Springs National Park taxable?

The park is federal land, established in 1921. A parcel near the line deserves a title company check.

Can a Garland County house with unpaid taxes still be sold?

Yes, provided the balance is paid at closing before any auction. Once the Commissioner of State Lands sells at auction, Act 241 makes it final.

Craighead County in brief

Northeast Arkansas holds Craighead County, crossed by Crowley's Ridge and run from two county seats: Jonesboro in the western district and Lake City in the eastern district. Jonesboro is the largest city. Other incorporated places include Bono, Black Oak, Caraway, Brookland, Monette, Bay, Egypt, Cash and Nettleton, which sits partly inside Jonesboro. The 2020 population was 111,231, and Arkansas State University is a major presence in the county.

A tax bill here depends on which city, school district and improvement district the parcel falls in, and not only on the county. Two houses with the same value can carry different bills.

Who sends the bill and who sets the value

Two offices do separate jobs. The Assessor decides what the property is worth. The Tax Collector sends the bill and takes the payment.

OfficeAddressPhone
Assessor511 S. Union St., Suite 130, Jonesboro870-933-4572
Tax Collector511 Union Street, Suite 107, Jonesboro; second office at 107 Cobean, Lake City870-933-4560

What the collector takes in goes to the County Treasurer at month's end, and the Treasurer hands it out. Schools get most of it. County offices, cities, fire and police pensions, libraries, roads, streets and improvement districts split the rest depending on where the parcel lies. Separately, the Assessor takes personal property reports, and the Circuit Clerk is where deeds and mortgages get recorded.

How the tax is calculated

Start with the Assessor's appraised value and take 20 percent of it. Multiply that taxable value by the millage rate where the house sits. A mill is a tenth of a cent. Local voters approve the rate.

Whoever owns the property of record on January 1 is assessed, and billing lags a year, so each assessment turns into a bill the following year. A sale in mid-year leaves the prior year's bill open until someone pays it, which the title company normally handles at closing.

Appraisers come back to each property every 3, 4 or 5 years and weigh size, quality and condition of improvements against sales and rental data. Tell the Assessor when you add a room, build a garage or start renting out a house you lived in.

Due dates and late penalties

Payment window: first business day of March to October 15 of the year after the assessment. Past that, taxes are delinquent, Arkansas Code 26-35-501 adds a 10 percent penalty, and interest builds daily on delinquent real estate. Mail counts as on time with an October 15 postmark. The collector advises buying postage at the counter or requesting a hand postmark, since a machine stamp can be dated later.

  • The county runs a payment portal for paying online.
  • For delinquent personal property, the office takes cash, money order, cashier's check or card (fees apply) and no personal checks.
  • The collector must publish delinquent lists each year. The personal property list goes to a local newspaper before December 1.

Personal property tax is its own account, yet an unpaid one can snag a payment day. Learn what sits under your name before you book a closing.

How to appeal an assessment

Call the Assessor first. Wrong square footage or a bad property description often gets fixed with no hearing. For a true value dispute, book a hearing with the County Board of Equalization by the third Monday in August. The board listens to you and decides whether to change the number. The Assessor's office has the current schedule and forms.

Homestead credit and freeze

A principal residence can earn the Amendment 79 homestead credit. Owners aged 65 or older, or totally disabled, can also ask for a freeze on taxable value. The credit was $600 at last report, and the legislature has considered raising it, so check with the Assessor before counting on a number.

Selling with taxes owed, step by step

Ask the Tax Collector for a payoff covering any older years too, and check for personal property tax under your name. The title company takes that total and pays the county out of what you would receive. Before closing, compare the legal description on the deed with the Assessor's parcel record so the recorded deed matches. After closing, give the collector your new mailing address so later notices reach you instead of the buyer.

Expect the title company to send you a payoff letter and a settlement statement that shows every charge. Read the statement before you sign. A cash buyer follows the same steps. With no lender involved, nothing waits on an appraisal, and the closing date depends on how fast the title work finishes.

Paperwork to gather

Carry the deed, your newest tax statement, photo ID and receipts for any additions. Landlords should add the lease and rent records. If the house is inherited, add the death certificate and any court papers. Two offices are in Jonesboro and one in Lake City, so choose the one nearest your side of the county.

Choosing the right office

With seats in two towns, it pays to know where to go. The Tax Collector keeps a main office in Jonesboro and a second office in Lake City, and the Assessor is in Jonesboro. A seller on the eastern side of the county can often finish the tax part of a sale at the Lake City office and save a trip. Phone ahead to confirm hours and what each location can do, since not every service is offered in both places.

Title companies in the area deal with these offices daily, so a call from them for a payoff is routine. Tell them early which parcel and which owner name appear on the bill.

If taxes go unpaid

A long-unpaid bill can end in a land sale through the Arkansas Commissioner of State Lands, held as a regional auction covering Craighead and nearby counties. Opening bids equal the taxes, penalties and interest. You can redeem up to 4 p.m. on the last business day before the sale. Act 241, effective July 1, 2023, makes an auction sale final. Parcels that find no bidder go on an online list about 30 days afterward.

Selling first can stop the clock. A buyer who closes through a title company gets the bill paid from the proceeds, and nothing is left to certify.

What selling involves

The Circuit Clerk, who serves as county recorder, files the deed. Recording costs $15 for the first page and $5 for each page after, with a $300 cap on multi-instrument documents. The state adds a transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on deals above $100, and the contract settles who pays.

  • Obtain a tax statement or payoff from the Tax Collector.
  • See if personal property tax is owed under the owner's name.
  • Match the deed's legal description to the Assessor's parcel record.
  • Have the title company pay the tax and record the deed on one day.

Tenants in place? Pull the lease and rent records first. Buyers and title companies both request them.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Craighead County?

The county Tax Collector. Offices are on Union Street in Jonesboro (Suite 107) and on Cobean in Lake City, and the phone is 870-933-4560.

When is the Craighead County tax deadline?

October 15. Anything paid later is penalized 10 percent, and real estate also accrues daily interest.

Where do I start if my assessment looks wrong?

Call the County Assessor. If the value itself is the issue, ask the County Board of Equalization for a hearing, which must be scheduled by the third Monday in August.

Is a mailed check on time with an October 15 postmark?

It is. Arkansas Code 26-35-501(c)(3)(A) covers that, and the collector suggests a hand postmark from the counter so the date is clear.

Can a house with back taxes still be sold?

Yes. The balance comes out of the proceeds at closing. Settle it before any state auction date, because an auction sale is final.

Benton County at a glance

Benton County fills the far northwest corner of Arkansas, on the Springfield Plateau of the Ozarks, with Missouri to the north and Oklahoma to the west. Bentonville is the county seat and Rogers is the largest city. Other communities include Bella Vista, Bethel Heights, Cave Springs, Centerton, Decatur, Gentry, Gravette, Little Flock, Lowell, Pea Ridge, Siloam Springs and Sulphur Springs. Springdale and Elm Springs lie mostly in Washington County, though parts reach into Benton.

Walmart, headquartered in Bentonville, is the largest single influence, and growth has followed the jobs: 153,406 in 2000, 221,339 in 2010 and 284,333 in 2020. The 2025 estimate is 332,554.   • Adding on to a home removes the freeze and reapplies it at the new value.

Home-based businesses are taxable, and business personal property tax is due October 15, paid one year behind.

Due dates and how to pay

Taxes are due by 11:59 p.m. on October 15. After that date a 10 percent late fee and or interest applies. The collector's calendar has tax books opening the first business day of March, May 31 as the deadline to assess, and July 1 as the last day to mail statements.

  • Online payment is open for current taxes, with a third-party fee of $3.99 for charges up to $110 and 3.59 percent above that.

  • E-checks and phone payments have not been accepted since November 1, 2019.
  • A tax information request form for title companies is on the collector's site, which helps at closing.

How to appeal your value

Values come from the assessor. Disputes go to the county equalization board. Section 26-27-317 allows you to apply up to the third Monday in August, and you are owed written notice of the decision after the hearing.

Storm repairs and selling as-is

An EF3 tornado 1.8 miles wide struck the county on May 26, 2024. If your house was hit or repaired, a buyer will ask whether the work was finished before listing. With values up 67.5 percent in the last reappraisal, many owners have more equity than they expect, and buyers have seen the same numbers. Price from recent sales of similar houses, not from the assessed value, since the assessment is only a share of the appraisal. List with your tax receipt in hand so a buyer can see exactly what the yearly bill has been, and be ready to explain whether caps or a freeze applied to your parcel.

If you are close to the October 15 deadline when you list, pay the current bill first. An open balance at the title stage slows everything down and gives a buyer a reason to ask for a credit.

Terrain and your house

The county sits on karst, so springs, sinkholes and caves are part of the ground under many lots. Houses near protected land, such as Pea Ridge National Military Park or Hobbs State Park-Conservation Area, or along Beaver Lake, can have lot shapes, slopes and access roads that differ from a flat subdivision lot. Ask an inspector about drainage and the foundation on such a property before you list.

Step by step: listing to closing

Begin with the tax record: look up your parcel, print the receipts and note the last appraised value. Then choose how to sell, with an agent or through a direct cash offer. When an offer is accepted, the title company opens a file and sends the tax information request form to the collector. The collector's answer shows what is owed for the current year and any earlier years. At closing you sign the deed, the county is paid from your proceeds, and you receive what remains.

Cash buyers remove the lender from the middle, so there is no appraisal wait and no repair list from a loan underwriter. That is especially useful for a storm-repaired house or a rental with deferred upkeep.

Paperwork to gather

Pull the deed, your last tax receipt, any equalization board notice and records of repairs or additions. If you added on to the home, say so, since an addition removes the freeze and reapplies it at the new value, and a buyer may ask. Homestead credit holders should tell the buyer that the credit does not carry over. Heirs should have the death certificate and court papers ready, and landlords should bring leases and a list of any damage claims.

Selling with taxes owed

Taxes owed can be paid at closing. Ask the collector for the balance, use the title information request form on the collector's site, and give the figure to the closing agent. A sale also restarts the assessment clock for a new owner, so a seller in Bentonville, Rogers or Bella Vista should know the house's last appraised value and when the next county-wide reappraisal is due.

Few sellers think about getting around, yet buyers from out of state do. US 62 and US 71 run through the county, and Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) is near Highfill, which helps out-of-town buyers.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Benton County property tax deadline?

October 15 at 11:59 p.m. After that, a 10 percent late fee and or interest applies.

Who handles property tax appeals in Benton County?

The assessor sets value and the county equalization board hears appeals. An owner may apply to the board on or before the third Monday in August.

Does the homestead credit transfer to a buyer?

No. The credit is for a primary residence, one per calendar year, and a buyer must apply on their own. A buyer who gets title by sale cannot claim an assessment limitation until the second assessment date after the transfer.

How can I get a tax figure for a closing?

The collector's website has a tax information request form for title companies, along with a tax record search where you can print receipts.

Is there a fee to pay Benton County taxes by card?

Yes. The online vendor charges $3.99 for payments of $110 or less and 3.59 percent above $110.

Pulaski County at a glance

Pulaski County is Arkansas's most populous, with 399,125 residents in 2020 and an estimate of 404,611 for 2025, and Little Rock is both its seat and the state capital. One assessor and one treasurer serve all of them, but neighborhoods, school districts and city rules differ a great deal from one to the next.

Jacksonville left the Pulaski County Special School District after voters approved the separation on September 16, 2014, and the Jacksonville North Pulaski School District began on July 1, 2016. The special district still serves other parts of the county, so confirm the district for your address before you describe the house to a buyer.

How to appeal your assessment

Assessment notices go out in July, and the clerk's office begins scheduling Equalization Board appointments around the same time. The last day to schedule a hearing is the third Monday in August. After the board's regular meetings, which run through the end of September, you can take an appeal to County Court by the second Monday in October.

The board holds a first meeting in early August to organize and receive the real and personal assessment rolls. It may meet in special session starting in October if needed, and when the ratio of assessed value to market value falls short a special session can run into the third Monday in November. Because the dates shift slightly, confirm them with the clerk each year.

Arrive with evidence. The owner carries the burden of showing the value is wrong, and comparable sales, photographs of defects and repair estimates are the usual proof.

Caps, homestead credit and the senior freeze

Arkansas caps the yearly increase in taxable value at 5 percent for a homestead and 10 percent for other real property. Under Amendment 79, the caps hold until the property reaches full assessed value. They do not apply to new construction, newly discovered property or substantial improvements, meaning renovations that add 25 percent or more to value.

Landlords feel the 10 percent cap on non-homestead property most. A rental valued well under market at the last reappraisal keeps climbing by that much every year until the gap closes, which a buyer of an investment house will notice.

Living in the house earns you the homestead credit: up to $500 a year, rising to up to $600 on 2026 bills. Age 65 or older, or a disability, can also freeze taxable value. That protection is yours alone. Whoever buys from you starts at the current value and may pay more than you did.

Then gather two or three recent sales of houses close to yours in size and age. Photographs of a failing roof, a cracked slab or water damage back up a request for a lower value. If you have a repair estimate, bring it too.

Selling with taxes owed

Arkansas collects property tax in the year after the assessment, so a Pulaski County closing often falls while a bill is unpaid or has not been issued yet. Ask the closing agent how the bill will be divided between seller and buyer and get the figure in writing.

Back taxes are the usual complication. If the property is behind, ask the Treasurer for a full payoff, including penalty and fees, so the title company can settle it from the sale proceeds. The state also charges a transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on transactions over $100, under Ark. Code 26-60-101 and following, and the state sells the transfer stamps.

Neighborhoods and condition

Little Rock's neighborhoods include The Heights, Hillcrest and Pleasant Valley, and the Quapaw Quarter holds three National Register historic districts. Other listed districts are Capitol-Main, Central High School and MacArthur Park. A house inside one of them can give a buyer pause, so find out early whether yours is.

The humid climate shows up as moisture in roofs, crawl spaces and bathroom floors, and a buyer who orders an inspection will look at each. Older Little Rock and North Little Rock houses with moisture damage can be hard to sell through a retail listing.

Situations sellers bring to us

  • A rental with tenants in place and a reappraisal notice showing a higher value.
  • A house in a listed historic district that a buyer may hesitate over.
  • An owner relocating on short notice for a job at a hospital, bank or the air base.

A direct sale to a buyer who purchases as is takes repairs and showings out of the timeline. The price still reflects condition, so compare any written offer with the tax and lien payoff on your statement to see the net.

Selling a rental or an inherited house

Tenants and heirs add steps. If a tenant lives in the house, tell the title company and share the lease so the buyer sees the term and rent. If several heirs own it, everyone has to sign the deed, and an out-of-town heir can often sign by mail or through a notary.

An inherited house that nobody lives in tends to collect unpaid tax. Ask the Treasurer for the full balance early and decide whether you will pay it first or let the closing do it. The longer it stays unpaid, the more penalty and fees ride along on the payoff.

From offer to closing

Once an offer is accepted, the title company searches the record and asks the Treasurer for the payoff. Gather the last tax statement, the deed and any notices from the assessor. If you rent the house out, have the lease ready so the buyer sees it.

At the table you sign the deed. The title company pays the Treasurer from proceeds, buys the transfer stamps, files the deed with the clerk and hands you the balance. With no lender involved, a cash sale can close faster, though it can still depend on how clean the title search is.

Call the Assessor at 501-340-6170, or visit 201 S. Broadway, Suite 310 in Little Rock. The County Clerk at 501-340-8500 schedules Equalization Board hearings.

What is the last day to appeal a Pulaski County assessment?

The third Monday in August is the last day to schedule an Equalization Board hearing. A further appeal to County Court is due by the second Monday in October.

Is Pulaski County on a four year reappraisal cycle?

Yes, the cycle ends in 2026. County staff do the work themselves across 177,110 parcels.

Does my senior tax freeze go to the buyer if I sell?

No. It stays with you. The buyer's taxable value resets at the next assessment.

Can I sell a Pulaski County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. Back taxes are normally paid out of the proceeds. Phone the Treasurer at 501-340-8345 for a payoff figure before you sign.

Who runs property tax

Work is divided among three offices: the assessor sets values, the County Clerk's office handles requests to the equalization board, and the collector sends bills and takes payment. The collector's office is at #8 East 7th Street, Mountain Home, AR 72653, phone 870-425-8300, with live support Monday through Friday, 8:00 to 4:30. The courthouse is at 1 East 7th Street.

The last round raised values 35 percent across residential, commercial and new construction in 2022. That is market value, not what owners paid, and caps and freezes keep taxes from rising at the same rate.

Due dates and penalties

The collector takes payments starting the first business day of March and stops counting a bill as timely on October 15. After that date, real or personal property tax is delinquent and a 10 percent penalty is added.

When tax stays unpaid

Years of unpaid real estate tax can send the land to the Commissioner of State Lands, which sets up a sale. Section 26-37-301 requires the Commissioner to notify the owner and anyone with a recorded interest, and to allow redemption once all taxes, penalties, interest and costs are paid.

A sale cannot be held until a year after certification. When the property is a homestead and nothing proves the owner got the certified letter, personal service must be arranged at least 60 days ahead of the sale. Someone with no ownership interest may redeem too, by paying what is due.

If your value is likely to rise, buyers may notice before you do. A new notice shows up in July, and a buyer who sees a higher assessed value may expect a higher bill. A complete folder lets the title company move quickly and prevents the most common closing delays.

No interstate crosses the county. US 62 and US 412 run together east to west, and Arkansas 5 is the only route running north to south throughout. October 15. The collector accepts payment from the first business day of March through that date, and unpaid tax is delinquent afterward with a 10 percent penalty.

The assessor and the collector each keep an office in both towns, so a seller in the north can handle paperwork in Stuttgart and a seller in the south can use DeWitt. People and housing

Selling the house resets nothing. Tax stays attached to the parcel, so a September closing with the year's bill unpaid means the collector's balance gets settled through the closing.

Market value is the standard. The assessor revisits each property on a cycle of three, four or five years and may compare sales, estimate cost or look at income. If the record shows the wrong square footage or room count, a phone call to the assessor frequently fixes it with no formal appeal.

Still unhappy? Book a hearing before the county board of equalization no later than the third Monday in August. Should the board rule against you, County Court is the next step, then Circuit Court.

Inheritance, tenants and transfer tax

A modest estate may qualify for the small estate procedure. Ark. Code 28-41-101 caps it at $100,000 and requires a 45-day wait plus a published notice to creditors when real property is involved.

A tenant-occupied house follows the state's landlord-tenant rules. A landlord may end an oral lease with one rental period's notice, or as the written lease provides.

Owners over 65 or disabled should bring proof of any freeze, and anyone who claimed the homestead credit should say so, because the new owner will have to apply on their own.

From the first business day of March through October 15. Taxes unpaid after October 15 are delinquent and carry a 10% penalty.

There are two. Stuttgart serves the northern district and DeWitt serves the southern district.

Unincorporated communities such as Center Hill, Joy, Liberty Valley, Providence and Plainview have their own mailing identities but no city government. Those places affect which millage rates land on your bill. Eight public school districts serve the county: Searcy, Beebe, Riverview, Bald Knob, White County Central, Pangburn, Rose Bud and Bradford. School millage follows the district, so find the district name on your tax statement before you list or take an offer.

White County offices and phone numbers

Every property tax bill passes through three offices. Values come from the assessor, bills and payments go through the collector, and the circuit clerk records the deed when a house changes hands.

OfficeAddress and phoneWhat it handles
White County Assessor119 West Arch, Searcy; real estate 501-279-6208, personal property 501-279-6205Valuation, reappraisal, homestead credit, personal property filing
White County Collector115 W. Arch Ave, Searcy; 501-279-6206Tax bills and payments, tax receipts for vehicle tags
White County Circuit ClerkWhite County Courthouse, 300 North Spruce, Searcy; 501-279-6203 or 501-279-6223Recording deeds, mortgages and liens as ex-officio recorder

All three offices open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. You can also pay the collector online by way of the county's tax search page, where credit cards carry a fee.

Assessment cycle and tax dates

Real property across the county is reappraised every five years, with a switch to a four-year cycle on January 1, 2027. Assessed value equals 20 percent of market value. Multiply the taxable assessed value by each taxing unit's millage rate and you have the bill.

Field staff go out at least yearly to find new construction, and since 2015 the county has contracted with Total Assessment Solutions Corporation. A new garage, a finished basement or a removed mobile home will show up in the record in time. Fix any mismatch yourself before a buyer's title company spots it.

  • January 1 to May 31: window to assess personal property such as vehicles, boats, trailers and business assets. A 10 percent late penalty applies afterward.
  • First business day of March to October 15: real and personal property tax is accepted without penalty.
  • Third Monday in August: final day to appeal this year's assessment.
  • October 15: last day to pay, and to apply for the Homestead Credit.

Homestead credit and caps

A Homestead Credit can take up to $425 off a bill. The Real Estate Department, at 501-279-6208, can confirm today's amount before you count on it. Qualified owners who are 65 or older, or disabled, can have their valuation frozen by the assessor.

State limits hold yearly increases to 5 percent on homesteads and 10 percent on other property. Miss October 15 and a 10 percent penalty follows.

What happens to property tax when you sell

Because Arkansas bills a year behind, someone who sells in spring still owes tax on the prior assessment. The tax is due by October 15 of the year after assessment, so the title company will ask for a current paid receipt or split the bill at closing.

Some habits that help:

  • Get the status of the latest bill from the collector before listing, rather than after a contract is signed.
  • See whether a homestead application was filed. Without the credit the bill runs higher than a buyer expects.
  • Mention any mobile home or trailer on the lot to the title company, because it is assessed apart from the land.
  • A partial payment does not close the account. The collector takes partial payments on current taxes, yet only a zero balance clears the file.

The transfer itself is taxed too. The state charges $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on deals above $100, paid with a transfer stamp, and the contract should name who buys it.

How deeds are recorded

Under Arkansas Code 14-15-402 the circuit clerk doubles as ex-officio county recorder. Deeds, mortgages, liens and surety bonds for county property are filed at the White County Courthouse, 300 North Spruce, in Searcy.

Title companies often record electronically through CSC, Simplifile or ePN, all of which the county accepts. A fraud alert program lets an owner register online and get an email whenever a document is recorded under their name, business name or trust. Heirs who have not yet retitled an inherited house should consider it.

Ask the clerk's office for the current recording fee before mailing a check.

Selling a White County house with a balance due

A tax balance does not stop a sale. It does need a number. Ask the collector for the payoff, hand it to the title company, and have it listed on the closing statement so it comes out of your proceeds. The buyer then receives a clean file, and you get the paid receipt.

If liens beyond taxes are on the property, the circuit clerk's records will show them. Check there early, so a lien recorded long ago does not surface during the title search.

If taxes go unpaid

Delinquent parcels are certified by the collector to the Arkansas Commissioner of State Lands and may in time be sold at public auction. The Commissioner must notify interested parties, lienholders of record at certification among them.

The minimum bid at auction is the tax owed, and live auctions turn down cash. A parcel that draws no buyer becomes available 30 days later. When one sells for more than the taxes, penalties, interest, fees and costs, a former owner who proves ownership at the time of sale can claim the excess one year afterward.

Behind on payments? Call the collector first and ask what balance would clear the account so a sale can close.

Papers to bring to the county offices

A single trip to Searcy can cover most of the errands. Carry the deed, a photo ID and your latest tax statement. At the assessor, check the record against your house. At the collector, ask for the balance and any receipts. At the circuit clerk, ask what documents are recorded against the property, and sign up for the fraud alert if you inherited the house.

Keep notes of what each office tells you, with the date, so the title company can match them to its own search.

Rural lots, wells and septic

Out in the country a house may run on a well and a septic system, and that usually adds a separate inspection before closing. Deferred repairs, a lien or an unresolved tax balance do not rule out an as-is cash sale. The offices above can each tell you which paperwork they handle.

Frequently asked questions

When are White County property taxes due?

Payment opens the first business day of March and runs through October 15 without penalty. A missed October 15 deadline brings a 10 percent penalty.

What is the deadline to appeal a White County assessment?

By the third Monday in August, to the county Board of Equalization. Further appeals go to county court and then circuit court.

Where do I pay White County property taxes?

Visit the White County Collector at 115 W. Arch Ave in Searcy on weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., or pay online (cards carry a fee). The collector's phone is 501-279-6206.

Does White County offer a homestead credit?

Yes, worth up to $425 off the bill, with applications due by October 15. The Real Estate Department at 501-279-6208 can confirm the current figure.

Who records a deed in White County?

The Circuit Clerk, acting as ex-officio county recorder, at 300 North Spruce in Searcy. CSC, Simplifile and ePN are accepted for electronic filing.

Conway County at a glance

Conway County lies in the Arkansas River Valley of central Arkansas, about 52 miles northwest of Little Rock. Morrilton is the county seat and largest city, with 6,992 residents in 2020. Plumerville and Oppelo are the incorporated towns. Conway the city is a different place, in Faulkner County to the east.

Census takers found 20,715 people in 8,387 households in 2020, and the 2025 estimate stands at 21,393. Vacancy hit 13.1 percent of the 9,646 housing units, and owners live in 73.2 percent of the occupied ones. Population slid 2.6 percent over the decade ending in 2020. Median age is 42.1, and 30.6 percent of residents live in urban areas. Most county offices, the courts and the assessor are in Morrilton, where Interstate 40 runs along the north side of the city and US 64 is the main road through downtown.

Manufacturing matters to demand. Green Bay Packaging announced a project of more than $1 billion at its Morrilton mill in June 2025, with 35 new jobs and a mill that already employs more than 620 people in the county.

Assessor and collector offices

The assessor and the collector share one address, 117 S. Moose Street in Morrilton, AR 72110. Assessor hours run Monday through Friday, 8:00 to 4:30, and the number is (501) 354-9622. Under section 26-26-715 the assessor must keep appraisal and assessment records current, so a change in land use or a new improvement should lead to an updated value.

The county collector collects property taxes for the county, its municipalities, the public schools, the library and improvement districts. Both offices link to the actDataScout vendor for tax and real estate record searches. The state is moving counties to a four-year reappraisal cycle, so ask the assessor when this county's next one falls. Yearly increases stop at 5 percent on a primary residence and 10 percent on commercial property.

How to appeal a valuation

Your application to the county equalization board is due by the third Monday in August. Hearings under section 26-27-317 must start by the second Monday of that month, and you can attend in person or submit documents instead.

  • Expect a written decision at least ten business days after the hearing.
  • That notice has to explain your right to go to county court and give the deadline.
  • Evidence that reaches the assessor fewer than five business days before the hearing may cause a continuance.
  • A petition filed for a business entity must be signed and filed by an Arkansas attorney.

Payment deadline

Collectors across Arkansas generally set October 15 as the deadline and add a 10 percent penalty afterward. Phone Conway County's collector for this county's dates and payment methods, and ask if any older years are still open on the parcel.

If taxes go unpaid

Land with unpaid tax may in time be certified to the Commissioner of State Lands, who has to notify the owner and offer redemption. Under section 26-37-301 the owner, or a person with no ownership interest, redeems by paying taxes, penalties, interest and costs, notice costs included.

  • No sale can occur until a year after certification.
  • Notice goes by certified mail first, then by regular mail if the certified letter is unclaimed or refused.
  • If a homestead owner cannot be shown to have received it, personal service is required at least 60 days before the sale.

Calling the collector sooner gets you a payoff number while choices remain.

Selling with back taxes

Back tax gets settled inside the sale. The collector tells you what is owed, penalty included, and the title company pays that from your proceeds when you close. Bring the deed and photo ID. If the owner has died and no probate has started, expect the title company to ask who has authority to sign before it can close.

Steps from decision to closing

First, decide whether to list with an agent or ask a cash buyer for an offer. Second, get the numbers: the tax balance from the collector and the assessed values from the assessor. Third, gather the deed and any records of repairs. Fourth, once an offer is accepted, the title company searches the record for liens and unpaid tax and sets the signing date. Fifth, you sign the deed, the county is paid from your proceeds and the sale is recorded.

Vacant houses and inherited houses need extra care. Utilities should stay on so a buyer can inspect the house, the roof and crawl space should be checked for water, and every heir should be reachable. A cash buyer can often work around these problems, but the title company still needs every signature.

Pricing a house that has been empty

A house that has sat vacant carries a discount in buyers' minds, so address it directly. Turn the water and power on for showings, clear debris from the yard, and have someone check for leaks and pests. Photos taken in daylight with the lights on do more than a long description. Be upfront about repairs and their cost, a buyer who finds a problem late tends to ask for a bigger credit than the repair would cost.

Some owners also ask a friend or neighbor to open the house for showings when they live far away. If cash is tight, selling as-is to a cash buyer avoids spending money on work you may not recoup.

Paperwork to gather

Keep the deed, the latest tax statement, any notice from the equalization board and receipts for work done on the house in one folder. If the owner died, add the death certificate and any court papers. If the house is a rental, add the lease and a note on the tenant's status. Updating the assessor on improvements ahead of time avoids surprises, since the assessor must keep records current when improvements change.

What sellers here usually face

With 13.1 percent of housing units vacant, many sellers here are dealing with houses that have sat empty. Morrilton gets about 51.20 inches of precipitation a year, so roofs, gutters and crawl spaces take steady moisture, and buyers look closely at them.

  • Houses sitting vacant after a death or a move.
  • Owners who cannot find the cash for roof, foundation or plumbing repairs.
  • Rental properties with a tenant who has left or stopped paying.
  • Back taxes tied to a probate that has not started.

A cash sale takes the house as it is and clears taxes from the proceeds, so repairs and the lender's appraisal do not hold up the closing.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Conway County property tax?

At the county collector's office at 117 S. Moose Street in Morrilton, AR 72110. An online tax record search is also available through actDataScout.

What is the deadline to appeal a Conway County assessment?

The third Monday in August under Ark. Code 26-27-317. The application goes to the county equalization board, which must start hearing appeals by the second Monday in August.

How big is Conway County?

About 567 square miles, among the smallest counties in Arkansas. It had 20,715 residents in the 2020 census.

Is Conway County the same as the city of Conway?

No. Conway County's seat is Morrilton. The city of Conway is in Faulkner County, which borders Conway County to the east.

Can I sell a house in Conway County with back taxes?

Yes. Ask the collector for the amount owed, including penalty, and settle it as part of the sale.
